schools.summary: Calvin makes the complaint of being forgotten faith's very exercise, not its failure — the eyes of the mind, guided by faith, penetrate to grace hidden in darkness; Gill: God seems to forget when he delays deliverance, but cannot forget the children for whom a book of remembrance is written.

Keil and Delitzsch hear three strophes of decreasing 'waves,' and with Hitzig set the psalm in Saul's persecution; Ellicott judges the double question unnecessary, rendering 'how long wilt thou continue to forget me.'
Clarke marks the fourfold 'how long' over the first two verses as deep dejection and earnestness, and reads 'hide thy face' as the want of any clear sense of God's approbation.

Henry: David construed the delay as unkindness, a peevish expression of prevailing fear, yet was a type of Christ's cry from the cross; Spurgeon feels intense desire mixed with impatience, yet checks it — 'Can God forget? Can Omniscience fail in memory?'
Augustine reads 'unto the end' as Christ the end of the law, and the cry to be forgotten 'unto the end' as the soul's longing to understand Christ, the Wisdom of God.

debates.question: On what occasion of David's life was the psalm composed?

sides.position: during Saul's persecution, when David was hunted from place to place
holders: Hitzig (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: during Absalom's conspiracy, after David's great sin
holders: an earlier expositor (as reported by Calvin)

sides.position: far later, in the captivity, as the prayer of worn-out Israel

outliers.note: Reads the whole heading and opening cry Christologically — 'unto the end' is Christ the end of the law, and to be 'forgotten unto the end' is to be delayed in the spiritual understanding of Christ.

themes: how long wilt thou forget me

schools.summary: Gill sets aside the good sense of taking counsel and hears a man at his wits' end, framing device after device, left to be his own and only counsellor.

Clarke: the soul frames ways and means that come to naught, schemes of self-recovery that cannot speak peace, while 'mine enemy' (Satan) triumphs under the curse of a broken law; Wesley: 'such perplexities, not knowing what course to take.'

Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain sense of daily sorrow against God's seeming ignorance; Ellicott doubts that 'soul' can mean the mind and renders 'form plans against my soul,' suspecting the psalmist had contemplated suicide.
Augustine turns 'place counsel in my soul' into an answer to the opening cry — how long shall I be in adversity? — with 'day' standing for the whole stretch of time the soul longs to be free of.

debates.question: What is the 'counsel' David takes in his soul?

sides.position: the frustrated devices and plans of a man in perplexity, at his wits' end
plans laid against his own life — a hint that suicide had entered his thoughts

outliers.note: Reads the verse allegorically — the counsel in the soul is the counsel of adversity, and 'through the day' means the whole of time from which the soul longs to rise to things eternal.

schools.summary: Gill hears David claim a covenant interest darkness had not cancelled, begging God to 'consider' his affliction, weakness, and enemies, and to 'hear' so as to answer at once.

Spurgeon: prayer lifts its voice like a watchman at daybreak; 'O Lord my God' proves our interest in God is not destroyed by trials; 'lighten mine eyes' = the eye of faith, of watchfulness, and of understanding.

Keil and Delitzsch read the lightening of the eyes as the imparting of new life, the brightness answering to the light of God's countenance (Ezra 9:8; 1 Sam. 14:27); Ellicott renders 'that I may not go to sleep in death,' the 'sleep unto death' of the LXX (Ps. 6:5).

Wesley: 'revive and comfort, and deliver me from the darkness of death'; Clarke presses 'consider and hear me' to 'answer me' — lost without thee, life drawing nigh to destruction, if I die unforgiven I die eternally.

themes: O LORD my God, the covenant cry
lest I sleep the sleep of death

schools.summary: Gill: an argument God himself takes notice of; the Chaldee turns the 'enemy' inward to indwelling corruption personified (as the apostle personifies sin), or applies it to Satan who triumphs when his temptation succeeds.
Clarke reads the enemy as Satan, who urges to sin then triumphs by insults; 'when I am moved' = moved from steadfastness and overcome — the desolation of a righteous soul's fall.
Henry keeps the enemy nearer — Saul or Satan gratified in David's fall ('So would I have it') — and hears David plead God's honour more than his own, lest the wicked trample on all that is sacred.
Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the hinge where lament and prayer give way to joyous anticipation, the emphatic 'but I' setting David against foes who desire his death.

themes: lest mine enemy say I have prevailed

schools.summary: Gill traces the ascent from complaining to praying to believing, David trusting not in himself or his merits but in the mercy of God as displayed in the plenteous redemption by Christ.

Henry marvels at the change from despair to praise; God's mercy is the support of faith, an anchor in a storm by which, though tossed, he was not overset, and joy in salvation comes by believing (Rom. 15:13).

Clarke reads the trust as a plea against falling ('wilt thou not once more lift up the light of thy countenance and cover my sin?'); there is no true joy but of the heart, which cannot rejoice till guilt is gone.

Ellicott hears the emphatic 'but as for me' and the Hebrew's restful cadence ('it hath a dying fall'); Keil and Delitzsch fix 'trusted' as faith clinging fast and the voluntative 'shall rejoice' as presupposing the sure realisation of hope.

outliers.note: Notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate carry an additional clause, found in no manuscript, 'yea, I will praise the name of the Lord most high.'

themes: but I have trusted in thy mercy
mercy the anchor in a storm
my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation

schools.summary: Gill reads the song as the fruit of believing: faith encouraged in prayer fills the heart with a joy the lips must express in praise, ascribing the glory of salvation to the Lord.

Clarke: that heart praises which has a clear sense of God's favour; 'dealt bountifully' = 'recompensed me,' a moment of spiritual joy worth a year of sorrow, oil of joy for heaviness — and he cites an old Scottish manuscript Psalter as proof of one Christian experience in all ages; Wesley: prophets speak of future deliverances as already come, for certainty and assurance.

Keil and Delitzsch take the perfect tense of a celebration that follows the fact which inspires it (Ps. 116:7); with the two closing iambics the song sinks to rest, peace reigning in the storm-tossed soul.
Henry hears David speak of the salvation as already past because by faith he had received its earnest and was as confident as if it were done.

debates.question: Why is the deliverance spoken of as already past ('he hath dealt bountifully')?

sides.position: the celebration follows the fact that inspires the song — the deliverance experienced
prophetic anticipation — a future deliverance spoken of as past by faith's assurance of its certainty

themes: I will sing unto the LORD
he hath dealt bountifully with me
